First
fŭrst
adj. & n. (foremost in order, rank, or time; rendering Hebrew ri'shon, Greek prōtos)
Saxon fyrst, superlative of fore. Scripture uses it three ways at once — first in sequence, first in rank, and First as a name of God.

Biblical Definition

First in Scripture is never merely the head of a list. It is an ordering God imposes and a title God claims. Christ says of Himself, “I am the first and the last” (Rev 1:17), and again, “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last” (Rev 22:13) — language the LORD had already used of Himself in Isaiah, so that the risen Christ is naming His own deity. Under that title everything else is sequenced. There is a first commandment, and our Lord identifies it: love to God with the whole heart is “the first and great commandment” (Mat 22:38), which means the whole moral law hangs on an order, not merely a list. There is a first man: “The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit” (1Co 15:45) — two federal heads, and every soul that has ever lived stands under one or the other. To be first in Scripture is therefore to be representative, to be determinative, to carry the rest along. This is why the firstborn is consecrated, why the firstfruits are brought before the harvest is touched, and why the kingdom must be sought first (Mat 6:33). The order is not arbitrary. God has arranged reality with a first, and to invert it is idolatry.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines first as advanced before or further than any other in progression, place, rank, dignity, or time — the ordinal of one.

expand to see more

FIRST, a. Advanced before or further than any other in progression; foremost in place; as the first man in a marching column.

2. Preceding all others in the order of time.

3. Preceding all others in numbers or a progressive series; the ordinal of one.

4. Preceding others in rank, dignity or excellence; chief; principal.

Key Scripture

Rev 1:17 — "And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as dead. And he laid his right hand upon me, saying unto me, Fear not; I am the first and the last:"

Rev 22:13 — "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last."

Mat 22:38 — "This is the first and great commandment."

1Co 15:45 — "And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit."

Modern Corruption

An age that has abolished rank has abolished first as a category — keeping the word for what happens earliest while denying that anything is owed the place of chief.

expand to see more

Modern usage keeps first as a stopwatch word and empties it of authority: first is whoever got there soonest, not what holds the place of chief by right. Scripture uses it the other way around. The first commandment is not first because Moses wrote it at the top of the tablet; it is first because God is God. Where the ordinal is flattened into mere sequence, the first commandment becomes one value among several to be balanced, and the balancing is done by the man doing the weighing — which is precisely the second commandment's definition of an idol.

The other loss is federal. “The first man Adam” is not an interesting datum about early history; he is the head under whom the race fell, and unless he is the real first man there is no coherent account of why we die or of how one Man's obedience could answer for many. Recover the ordinal and the gospel's logic returns: a first Adam who lost us, a last Adam who is a quickening spirit, and a first-and-last Christ who was dead and is alive for evermore.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ri'shon (H7223), first, chief, former; Greek prōtos (G4413), first in time, place, order, or importance — and the divine title in Revelation.

expand to see more

Hebrew ri'shon (H7223) — first, foremost, former; used of the first month (Exo 12:2), the first day, and the LORD as first (Isa 44:6).

Greek prōtos (G4413) — first in order or in rank; the first commandment (Mar 12:30), the first resurrection (Rev 20:5), and “I am the first and the last” (Rev 1:17).

Greek archē (G746) — beginning, origin, first place; paired with telos (end) in the title of Rev 22:13.

Usage

"“I am the first and the last” — the ordinal used as a divine name."

"“This is the first and great commandment” — the moral law has an order, and love to God heads it."

"“The first man Adam” — federal headship stated as a sequence."
